name: Fall of Ur (c. 2004 BCE)
other_names: Elamite sack of Ur; Lament for Ur
making_significance: Elamite and Shimashki forces sacked Ur and ended the Ur III state and its large textile and craft workshops, an event mourned in the Sumerian city laments.
leaves_out: the dependent workers of the Ur III workshops
free_sources: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Thera eruption (c. 1600 BCE)
date_note: date debated: radiocarbon c. 1600 BCE vs archaeological c. 1500 BCE
making_significance: The eruption buried the town of Akrotiri on Thera in ash, preserving painted walls, storage jars and multi-storey houses.
leaves_out: the people who left before the eruption, whose fate is unknown
notes: links: CIV074; POL115. Link to Minoan decline is debated.

name: Uluburun shipwreck (c. 1320 BCE)
making_significance: A ship that sank off southern Anatolia carried copper and tin ingots, glass ingots, ivory, ebony and jewellery, a snapshot of Late Bronze Age trade in raw materials.
leaves_out: the crew, whose origin is still debated

name: Late Bronze Age collapse (c. 1200–1150 BCE)
making_significance: Palaces from Mycenae to Hattusa and Ugarit fell, ending palace workshops and long-distance trade in copper, tin and glass, and writing stopped in Greece.
leaves_out: the non-palatial communities that carried on
notes: links: POL100; POL101; POL116; NET020. Causes debated (drought, earthquakes, raiders, system collapse).

name: Elamite seizure of Babylonian monuments (c. 1158 BCE)
other_names: Shutruk-Nahhunte's raid on Sippar and other cities
making_significance: The Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte carried Mesopotamian stelae, including the Code of Hammurabi and the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin, to Susa and re-inscribed some of them, an early recorded case of taking made monuments as trophies.
defined_by: Assyriologists and Elamologists from Susa excavations (French mission, 1898 on)
leaves_out: the craftsmen who carved and re-carved the stelae
free_sources: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports
notes: links: POL098; CIV059; TXT038. Stelae found at Susa by de Morgan's mission 1898–1902 and now in the Louvre.

name: Neo-Assyrian mass deportations (8th–7th c. BCE)
date_note: approx.; from Tiglath-pileser III to Ashurbanipal
making_significance: Assyrian kings moved hundreds of thousands of conquered people, often skilled craftsmen, to build and furnish their cities.
leaves_out: the deportees, shown only as captives in the reliefs
free_sources: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: links: POL096; STY169. Numbers in royal inscriptions are propaganda.

name: Fall of Nineveh (612 BCE)
making_significance: The sack of Nineveh by Babylonian and Median forces ended the Assyrian palace workshops, while fire baked clay tablets of the palace libraries and left carved wall reliefs buried until the 19th century.
leaves_out: deported craft workers of the Assyrian empire
free_sources: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: POL096; POL097. Relief removal to London in the 1840s–50s (Layard) is a later F1.24 story.

name: Cyrus Cylinder and the return of cult statues (539 BCE)
making_significance: After taking Babylon, Cyrus declared that he returned cult statues to their temples and resettled their peoples, a royal claim often read as an early "restitution".
leaves_out: the Babylonian priests who wrote it and the modern myths of "the first human-rights charter"
free_sources: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Twelve Tables funerary limits (c. 450 BCE)
other_names: Law of the Twelve Tables, Table X
date_note: approx.; text survives only in later quotations
making_significance: The early Roman law code capped funeral display, including numbers of mourning cloths and a ban on burying gold except gold bound to teeth.
defined_by: Roman state; reconstructed by modern philologists from Cicero and others
leaves_out: non-elite funerals, which left few records
notes: Cicero, De legibus 2.23–24 preserves the clauses.

name: Sack of Persepolis (330 BCE)
making_significance: Alexander's army looted the Achaemenid treasury and burned the palace complex, dispersing metalwork and ending the royal building workshops.
defined_by: historians (Diodorus, Plutarch, Arrian); archaeologists (Oriental Institute excavations 1931–39)
leaves_out: the multi-ethnic workforce named in the Persepolis Fortification Tablets
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Qin standardisation (221 BCE)
other_names: unification of script, weights, measures and axles
making_significance: After unifying China, the Qin state standardised script, coinage, weights, measures and axle widths, and stamped standard vessels with the edict.
functions: exchange and value;record and writing;rule and display
leaves_out: the regional scripts and measures it replaced
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Chinese Text Project (link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lex Oppia (215 BCE)
making_significance: A Roman sumptuary law passed during the Second Punic War limited women to half an ounce of gold and banned multi-coloured dress, so its repeal debate records how dress and jewellery signalled rank.
leaves_out: the women who protested for its repeal, known mainly through Livy
notes: Livy 34.1–8 gives the repeal debate (Cato vs Valerius).

name: Sack of Corinth (146 BCE)
other_names: destruction of Corinth by Lucius Mummius
making_significance: Roman troops sacked Corinth and shipped Greek statues and bronzes to Italy, feeding a Roman market for Greek art and copies.
leaves_out: enslaved Corinthians sold after the sack
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; public-domain primary texts
notes: links: POL120. "Corinthian bronze" as a luxury label in Pliny.

name: Zhang Qian's missions to the Western Regions (138–126 BCE)
date_note: first mission c. 138–126 BCE; second c. 119–115 BCE
making_significance: Han envoy Zhang Qian's journeys to Central Asia are traditionally taken as opening Han contact with the Western Regions and their horses, glass and metalwork.
leaves_out: the steppe and oasis peoples already trading
free_sources: Chinese Text Project (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Han salt and iron monopolies (117 BCE)
other_names: Debate on Salt and Iron (81 BCE)
date_note: monopolies from c. 117 BCE; debate 81 BCE
making_significance: Emperor Wu put salt making and iron casting under state monopoly, and a court debate in 81 BCE argued over the quality and price of state-made tools.
defined_by: Han state; Huan Kuan's Yantie lun
leaves_out: the conscript and convict labour in state foundries

name: Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE)
making_significance: Roman forces destroyed the Second Temple and carried its menorah and vessels to Rome, where the Arch of Titus shows them in procession.
leaves_out: captives enslaved after the siege

name: Eruption of Vesuvius (79 CE)
making_significance: Ash and pyroclastic flows buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, preserving workshops, bakeries, fulleries and painted rooms whose later excavation shaped knowledge of Roman making.
leaves_out: enslaved workers of the towns, prominent among the dead
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Met Open Access (CC0); public-domain primary texts
notes: links: STY006; TXT002. Excavation event listed separately (OCC097).

name: Shapur I's Roman captives (260)
making_significance: After capturing the emperor Valerian, Shapur I settled Roman prisoners in Iran, where they are credited with building dams and bridges such as the Band-e Kaisar at Shushtar.
leaves_out: the captives' own names and lives
notes: links: POL107. Engineering attribution is traditional.

name: Edict on Maximum Prices (301 CE)
making_significance: Diocletian's edict fixed prices for goods and wages across the empire, listing rates for purple dye, silk, textiles and the day-pay of builders, carpenters and painters.
leaves_out: makers paid by piece or in kind
free_sources: public-domain primary texts; Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports
notes: Known from inscribed copies, mostly in the eastern provinces.

name: Sack of Rome (410)
making_significance: Alaric's Visigoths looted Rome for three days, a shock that became a founding story for "the fall of Rome" and for Late Antique hoarding of silver.
leaves_out: the non-elite Romans and the Goths' own motives
notes: links: POL120. The "fall" narrative is contested (see PRD064).

name: Buddhism reaches the Yamato court (538 or 552)
other_names: gift of a Buddha image from Baekje
making_significance: Baekje's gift of a gilt-bronze Buddha and sutras to the Yamato court is the traditional start of Buddhism in Japan, followed by Baekje temple builders, tile makers and image makers.
leaves_out: the Korean craftsmen who built Asuka-dera
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons

name: Teotihuacan burning (c. 550)
making_significance: The civic and ritual centre of Teotihuacan was burned and its images smashed, ending the city's role as Mesoamerica's largest craft centre.
leaves_out: the causes, still unknown (internal revolt or attack)

name: Silkworms reach Byzantium (c. 552)
making_significance: Procopius tells of monks bringing silkworm eggs from Central Asia to Justinian, the traditional start of Byzantine sericulture.
leaves_out: Sogdian and Persian silk producers
notes: links: NET001; DIA001. A story, not a documented transfer; versions differ on who carried the eggs.

name: Tang robe-colour rules (630)
date_note: edict of the 8th month, Zhenguan 4 (630); revised later in the Tang
making_significance: An edict of 630 assigned robe colours to official ranks, purple for the third rank and above, crimson for the fourth and fifth, green for the sixth and seventh and blue for the eighth and ninth, making dyed cloth a visible mark of rank.
defined_by: Tang state; historians (Old and New Tang Histories)
leaves_out: commoners and dyers
free_sources: Chinese Text Project (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: Colour ladder quoted from the Zhenguan 4 edict in a Later Tang memorial (932); rules changed several times.

name: Coinage reform of ʿAbd al-Malik (696–697)
making_significance: The Umayyad caliph replaced Byzantine- and Sasanian-style coins with gold and silver coins bearing only Arabic inscriptions, setting a lasting epigraphic design for Islamic coinage.
leaves_out: the Byzantine- and Sasanian-trained mint workers whose designs it replaced
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: DYN009. Nomisma for coin types.

name: Byzantine Iconoclasm (726–843)
making_significance: Imperial bans on religious figural images led to destroyed or replaced icons and mosaics, and the 843 restoration fixed rules for icon painting that lasted.
leaves_out: iconophile monks' and women's roles, known from partisan sources
notes: links: BEL010; POL121. Sources are almost all from the victorious side.

name: Huichang persecution of Buddhism (845)
making_significance: Tang orders closed thousands of monasteries and melted bronze images and bells for coinage, destroying much Buddhist metalwork.
leaves_out: monks and nuns returned to lay life
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); public-domain primary texts

name: End of embassies to Tang (894)
making_significance: Japan's court stopped sending envoys to Tang China, a date later used to mark a turn to kokufū ("national style") court art.
leaves_out: continued private trade with China and Korea
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Japan Search
notes: links: STY145; PRD121. The "isolation" reading is now questioned.

name: Book of the Eparch (c. 912)
date_note: approx.; attributed to Leo VI; 911–912 is one reading of the date
making_significance: The Byzantine prefect's rulebook regulated Constantinople's guilds, including silk dealers and dyers, and barred export of reserved imperial silks.
leaves_out: workers outside the guilds
notes: links: TXT009; POL121. Event row for the edict; the text is TXT009.

name: Somnath raid (1026)
other_names: Mahmud of Ghazni's raid on Somnath
making_significance: Mahmud of Ghazni sacked the Somnath temple in Gujarat and carried off its treasure, an event later retold in competing nationalist histories.
defined_by: Persian chroniclers; colonial and nationalist historians
leaves_out: how the temple and town recovered, which later sources obscure
free_sources: public-domain primary texts; Indian Culture portal (per-owner licence)
notes: links: DYN014. See Romila Thapar, Somanatha (2004), on the event's later uses.

name: Fatimid treasury looting (1067–1069)
making_significance: Unpaid troops looted the Fatimid palace treasuries in Cairo, dispersing rock crystal, textiles, books and metalwork across the Mediterranean.
leaves_out: the palace craftsmen who made the objects
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: POL041; STY101. Many Fatimid rock crystals now in European church treasuries.

name: Jingkang incident (1127)
making_significance: Jurchen Jin forces took Kaifeng, capturing two Song emperors, the imperial collections and many artisans, and the Song court re-formed in the south.
leaves_out: artisans and palace women taken north
free_sources: National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0); Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)
notes: links: POL166; SCH034. Ru ware production ends with the Northern Song.

name: Destruction of Nalanda (c. 1193–1200)
making_significance: Nalanda and other monastic centres in Bihar were destroyed around 1200, ending workshops for Pala-style bronzes and palm-leaf manuscripts in the region.
leaves_out: the monks and craftsmen who moved to Nepal and Tibet
notes: links: POL191; STY119. Attribution to Bakhtiyar Khalji is common but debated.

name: Sack of Constantinople (1204)
making_significance: Crusaders looted Constantinople and carried relics, reliquaries, enamels and the bronze horses to Venice, filling western treasuries with Byzantine work.
leaves_out: the Byzantine makers whose work was melted down

name: Mongol deportations of artisans (1219–1260s)
making_significance: Mongol armies spared and relocated skilled craftsmen from conquered Central Asian and Iranian cities to workshops in Mongolia and China, mixing textile and metal traditions.
leaves_out: the named individuals behind "artisan households"
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)
notes: links: POL233; DYN074; NET001. Numbers in chronicles are unreliable.

name: Sack of Baghdad (1258)
making_significance: Hülegü's army sacked Baghdad and ended the Abbasid caliphate, destroying libraries and scattering craftsmen, though some later worked for the Ilkhans.
leaves_out: continuities in Baghdad's crafts after 1258
free_sources: Digital Library of the Middle East; Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: links: DYN010; POL234; STY103. Scale of library loss is often exaggerated.

name: Mansa Musa's hajj (1324)
making_significance: Mali's ruler travelled to Mecca through Cairo with large amounts of gold and brought back the Andalusi poet al-Sahili, whom Ibn Khaldun credits with an audience hall in Mali and later tradition with mosques at Timbuktu and Gao.
leaves_out: the enslaved people in the caravan
notes: links: POL036; CIV008; NET010. Architectural attributions to al-Sahili beyond the audience hall are weakly supported.

name: Black Death (1347–1351)
date_note: main wave; recurrences to the 18th century
making_significance: Plague killed perhaps a third to a half of the population in affected areas, raising wages for surviving craft workers and prompting labour laws.
leaves_out: non-European losses, less studied

name: Statute concerning Diet and Apparel (1363)
date_note: 1363; later Acts of Apparel (1533 etc.) repealed 1604
making_significance: English law set which cloths, furs and prices each rank could wear, one of a series of sumptuary acts that shaped the cloth trade.
leaves_out: the tailors and furriers who adapted to the rules
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Ming sumptuary regulations (from 1368)
date_note: approx.; rules reissued and widely broken
making_significance: Early Ming law restricted dragon and phoenix motifs, certain colours and gold embroidery to the court and set house sizes and decoration by rank.
leaves_out: merchants who ignored the rules as Ming commerce grew
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0)
notes: links: POL168. Rank badges (buzi) as members.

name: Ming maritime ban (1371–1567)
making_significance: The Ming ban on private sea trade pushed porcelain and silk exports into tribute missions and smuggling until its relaxation in 1567.
leaves_out: coastal traders labelled "pirates" (wokou)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (CC0/PDM)
notes: links: NET054; NET008; DIA007. Qing had a separate ban (see Great Clearance).

name: Timur's deportation of artisans (1398–1402)
making_significance: Timur forcibly moved builders, weavers, glass and metal workers from Delhi, Damascus and elsewhere to build and furnish Samarkand, as Clavijo saw in 1404.
leaves_out: the deported makers and their home cities

name: Zheng He's voyages (1405–1433)
making_significance: Seven Ming fleets carried porcelain, silk and gifts to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, recorded in the Liujiagang and Changle inscriptions.
defined_by: Ming records; Ma Huan's Yingya shenglan
leaves_out: the crews and the societies visited
notes: links: TXT089; TXT090; NET005. Ship sizes in later sources are disputed.

name: Ming occupation of Đại Việt (1407–1427)
making_significance: Ming armies removed books and took Vietnamese craftsmen to China, among them Nguyễn An, later credited with building work in Beijing.
leaves_out: the craftsmen named only collectively
notes: links: POL215. Nguyễn An's role in the Forbidden City to verify.

name: Hunminjeongeum promulgated (1446)
making_significance: King Sejong's court issued a designed alphabet for Korean, with the Haerye explaining letter shapes from the organs of speech.
leaves_out: the scribes and scholars who worked on it
free_sources: KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons; Kyujanggak / Uigwe (link-out)

name: Fall of Constantinople (1453)
making_significance: Ottoman conquest ended the Byzantine state; Greek scholars and makers moved west while Mehmed II rebuilt the city with new court workshops.
leaves_out: the city's people and continuities under Ottoman rule

name: Ōnin War (1467–1477)
making_significance: Fighting destroyed much of Kyoto; returning weavers settled near the old Western Army camp, which gave the Nishijin weaving district its name.
leaves_out: non-elite Kyoto residents
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Japan Search

name: Venetian Patent Statute (1474)
making_significance: Venice granted ten-year exclusive rights to makers of new and useful devices, an early general patent law.
leaves_out: guild members excluded from rights

name: Gyeongguk daejeon (1485)
making_significance: Joseon's law code registered government artisans by craft in the capital and provinces and set dress and household rules by rank.
leaves_out: artisans outside the registers

name: Portuguese brass in Benin (from c. 1485)
making_significance: Portuguese traders brought brass manillas to Benin, and metal analysis links many Benin brasses to manillas made in the Rhineland.
leaves_out: enslaved people traded in the same exchanges
notes: links: DYN038; POL026. Isotope study published 2023.

name: Alhambra Decree (1492)
other_names: expulsion of the Jews from Spain
making_significance: Spain's order expelling Jews scattered Sephardic silversmiths, weavers and printers to North Africa, the Ottoman empire and elsewhere.
leaves_out: those who converted and stayed

name: Columbus's first voyage and the Columbian exchange (1492)
making_significance: Columbus's landfall in the Caribbean began transfers of crops, animals, materials, diseases and people that remade making in the Americas and beyond.
leaves_out: Taíno and other Indigenous peoples first affected
free_sources: public-domain primary texts; Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain); Wikimedia Commons

name: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut (1498)
making_significance: The Portuguese sea route round Africa to India began direct European trade in Indian textiles and spices.
leaves_out: the Gujarati and Arab pilots and traders already on the route

name: Portuguese sack of Kilwa and Mombasa (1505)
other_names: Almeida's attacks on the Swahili coast
making_significance: Portuguese forces under Francisco de Almeida sacked Kilwa and Mombasa, disrupting the Swahili coast's gold and cloth trade.
leaves_out: Swahili accounts such as the Kilwa Chronicle

name: Ottoman deportation of artisans from Tabriz and Cairo (1514–1517)
making_significance: After taking Tabriz and Cairo, Selim I moved painters, tile makers, weavers and other craftsmen to Istanbul ("brought", in the source; historians also call it deportation), feeding the court workshops.
leaves_out: the deported makers' names outside payroll registers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0)

name: Epidemics in the Americas (from 1518)
making_significance: Introduced epidemics killed a large share of Indigenous people, destroying workshops and passing on fewer makers' skills.
leaves_out: the survivors who kept crafts going

name: Fall of Tenochtitlan (1521)
other_names: Spanish conquest of the Mexica capital
making_significance: The Spanish-led conquest, with Indigenous allies, destroyed Tenochtitlan, and most Mexica goldwork was melted into bars, so few pieces survive.
defined_by: historians; Spanish and Nahua sources (Florentine Codex)
leaves_out: the Tlaxcalan and other Indigenous allies; Mexica survivors
free_sources: INAH Mediateca (link-out); Wikimedia Commons; public-domain primary texts
notes: links: POL051; POL052; CIV020; TXT109; TXT114. Surviving featherwork (e.g. Vienna headdress) is a restitution case.

name: Ransom of Atahualpa (1532–1533)
making_significance: Inca gold and silver collected to ransom Atahualpa at Cajamarca were melted down by the Spanish, erasing most imperial metalwork.
leaves_out: the Andean smiths who made the pieces
free_sources: public-domain primary texts; Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536–1541)
making_significance: Henry VIII's closure of English and Welsh monasteries led to stripped lead, melted plate, broken shrines and scattered libraries.
leaves_out: lay workers dependent on monasteries
free_sources: British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons); Wikimedia Commons; Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images)

name: New Laws of the Indies (1542)
making_significance: Spanish law sought to end Indigenous enslavement and phase out the encomienda, changing how Indigenous labour for building and craft was demanded.
leaves_out: Indigenous and African people still coerced after the laws

name: Portuguese reach Tanegashima (1543)
other_names: arrival of the matchlock in Japan
making_significance: Portuguese traders brought matchlock guns to Tanegashima, and Japanese smiths are credited with copying them within a few years.
leaves_out: Chinese traders who carried the Portuguese
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Japan Search

name: Silver found at Potosí (1545)
making_significance: The silver mountain of Potosí became the largest silver source of its time, feeding mints, colonial silverwork and global trade.
leaves_out: Andean mitayos and enslaved Africans who worked the mines

name: Maní auto-da-fé (1562)
other_names: burning of Maya books at Maní
making_significance: Franciscan friar Diego de Landa burned Maya books and images at Maní, so only four Maya codices are known to survive.
leaves_out: Maya scribes and the knowledge in the books

name: Council of Trent decree on images (1563)
other_names: Decree on the invocation of saints and sacred images
making_significance: The Catholic Church's decree on images asked that religious art be clear, decorous and approved by bishops, shaping Counter-Reformation art in Europe and its colonies.
leaves_out: Indigenous and colonial makers who adapted the rules

name: Statute of Artificers (1563)
making_significance: English law made a seven-year apprenticeship compulsory in many trades and let justices set wages, framing craft training for 250 years.
leaves_out: women's household craft work, outside the statute
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Battle of Talikota and sack of Vijayanagara (1565)
making_significance: After defeat by a coalition of Deccan sultanates, Vijayanagara's capital at Hampi was looted and abandoned, ending its temple and palace workshops.
leaves_out: continuities in later Nayaka courts
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Indian Culture portal (per-owner licence)

name: Urdaneta's return route (1565)
making_significance: Andrés de Urdaneta found a return route across the Pacific, making the Manila–Acapulco galleon run possible.
leaves_out: Filipino and Chinese sailors and shipbuilders
notes: links: INS040; NET036. Event only; the trade itself is INS040/NET036.

name: Beeldenstorm (1566)
making_significance: Protestant crowds stripped and smashed images in hundreds of Low Countries churches.
leaves_out: Catholic makers and later restorers

name: Potosí mita reorganised (1573)
making_significance: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo imposed rotating forced labour drafts on Andean communities for the Potosí mines and mills.
leaves_out: the mitayos and their families

name: Sword hunt (1588)
making_significance: Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered farmers to give up swords and guns, fixing a line between armed samurai and unarmed commoners.
leaves_out: farmers who hid weapons
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Japan Search
notes: links: DYN070. Hideyoshi claimed the metal would be used for a Great Buddha.

name: Imjin War (1592–1598)
making_significance: Japanese invasions devastated Korea, and many Korean potters were taken to Japan, where they are credited with founding kilns such as those at Arita and Satsuma.
leaves_out: the captives who could not return
free_sources: KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons; ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Capture of the carracks São Jacinto and Santa Catarina (1602–1603)
making_significance: Dutch capture and auction of two Portuguese carracks put large lots of Chinese blue-and-white porcelain on the Amsterdam market, launching the "kraak" fashion.
leaves_out: the Jingdezhen potters

name: Deportation of Armenians from Julfa (1604–1605)
making_significance: Shah ʿAbbas forcibly moved the Armenians of Julfa to Isfahan, where New Julfa merchants and craftsmen ran a silk and textile network.
leaves_out: those who died in the march

name: Expulsion of the Moriscos (1609–1614)
making_significance: Spain expelled about 300,000 Moriscos, losing silk, pottery and building crafts that moved to North Africa.
leaves_out: Moriscos who stayed hidden

name: Extirpation of idolatry in Peru (1609–1660s)
making_significance: Church campaigns in the Andes seized and burned huacas, mallquis and ritual objects.
leaves_out: Andean communities who hid huacas

name: Statute of Monopolies (1624)
making_significance: English law ended most royal monopolies but kept patents for new inventions, the basis of later patent law.
leaves_out: inventors without means to petition
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Sakoku edicts (1633–1639)
making_significance: Tokugawa edicts limited foreign trade to Dutch and Chinese ships at Nagasaki and set the terms of Japan's porcelain and textile exports.
leaves_out: Ryukyu, Tsushima and Ainu trade
notes: links: INS025; POL183; DYN071. "Closed country" label is contested.

name: Queue order (1645)
making_significance: The Qing required Han men to shave the forehead, wear the queue and adopt Manchu-style dress, changing tailoring and hair work across China.
leaves_out: women, who were largely exempt
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0)

name: Navigation Acts (1651–1660)
making_significance: English law required colonial trade to use English ships, shaping what colonies could make and sell.
leaves_out: colonial makers barred from some trades
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts
notes: links: POL137. Enumerated goods included sugar and tobacco produced by enslaved people.

name: VOC's first large order for Japanese porcelain (1659)
making_significance: With Chinese supply disrupted, the VOC placed a large order at Arita, beginning Japanese export porcelain for Europe.
leaves_out: the Arita potters, many of Korean descent
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (CC0/PDM); Met Open Access (CC0); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)
notes: links: INS038; DIA012. Small purchases from the 1650s (4,149 pieces ordered 1656); the 1659 order was for 64,866 pieces.

name: Great Clearance (1661–1683)
making_significance: The Qing forced coastal people inland to cut off Zheng forces on Taiwan, disrupting coastal kilns, salt works and trade.
leaves_out: the displaced coastal people

name: Burial in Woollen Acts (1666–1680)
making_significance: English law required the dead to be buried in woollen shrouds, to support the wool trade.
leaves_out: linen weavers and importers, and families fined for using linen
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Great Fire of London (1666)
making_significance: After the fire, London rebuilt in brick and stone under the Rebuilding Act, with Wren's churches and new building rules.
leaves_out: the displaced poor
free_sources: Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images); British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons)

name: Royal edict founding the Gobelins manufactory (1667)
other_names: Manufacture royale des meubles de la Couronne
making_significance: Louis XIV's edict made the Gobelins a royal manufactory under Le Brun for tapestry, furniture and metalwork.
leaves_out: Flemish weavers and other migrant workers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Getty Museum Open Content (CC0); Paris Musées (Open Content)

name: Pueblo Revolt (1680)
making_significance: Pueblo peoples expelled Spanish colonists from New Mexico and destroyed mission churches, restoring kiva practice for a time.
leaves_out: Pueblo views of the event
free_sources: Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain); US National Archives Catalog

name: Tenna sumptuary edicts (1683)
making_significance: Shogunal edicts banned townspeople from wearing gold brocade, embroidery and full tie-dye (sō-kanoko), a ban often linked to the rise of yūzen paste-resist dyeing.
leaves_out: dyers and weavers who adapted
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: Link to yūzen's rise is a common but debated claim.

name: Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685)
making_significance: The revocation drove Huguenot silk weavers, silversmiths and watchmakers out of France to England, the Netherlands and Prussia.
leaves_out: those who converted and stayed
free_sources: public-domain primary texts; Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images)

name: French ban on printed calicoes (1686–1759)
making_significance: France banned import, making and wearing of printed cottons to protect silk and wool, while smuggling and illicit printing continued.
leaves_out: smugglers and illicit printers
free_sources: Paris Musées (Open Content); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Minas Gerais gold rush (1690s)
making_significance: Gold finds in Minas Gerais drew miners and enslaved Africans, funding gilded Baroque churches.
leaves_out: enslaved African miners and craftsmen
free_sources: BNDigital (Biblioteca Nacional do Brasil); Wikimedia Commons

name: Calico Act (1700)
other_names: An Act for the more effectual employing the poor...
making_significance: English law banned imports of printed, painted or dyed calicoes from Persia, China and the East Indies, protecting wool and silk and encouraging printing on imported plain cloth in England.
leaves_out: Indian dyers and printers who lost a market
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: NET055; INS030. Pair with OCC093.

name: Coke smelting at Coalbrookdale (1709)
making_significance: Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke instead of charcoal, which later made cheap cast iron pots, rails and bridges possible.
leaves_out: colliers and ironworkers
free_sources: Science Museum Group Collection (link-out); Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images)

name: Statute of Anne (1710)
making_significance: The first British copyright statute gave authors rather than printers a limited term of rights in books.
leaves_out: printers, engravers and designers, not covered until later acts
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Calico Act (1721)
making_significance: English law banned the wearing and household use of most printed calicoes, while fustians and muslins stayed legal, steering the growth of British cotton manufacture.
defined_by: English Parliament; wool and silk weavers' protests
leaves_out: Indian cloth producers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: NET055. Spitalfields weavers attacked calico-wearers in 1719–20.

name: Afghan sack of Isfahan (1722)
making_significance: The siege and fall of Isfahan to Afghan forces ended Safavid court patronage of carpets, textiles and painting.
leaves_out: the people who starved during the siege

name: İbrahim Müteferrika's press (1727)
other_names: first Ottoman Turkish printing press using Arabic type
making_significance: A licence from the sultan let İbrahim Müteferrika print books in Ottoman Turkish with movable Arabic type in Istanbul.
leaves_out: Jewish, Armenian and Greek printers active in Istanbul earlier
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Digital Library of the Middle East
notes: links: INV043. The claimed earlier Ottoman "print ban" is debated.

name: Engraving Copyright Act (1735)
making_significance: After campaigning by Hogarth and others, British law gave engravers copyright in their designs.
leaves_out: engravers working from others' designs, less protected
free_sources: Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images); official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out)

name: Herculaneum and Pompeii excavations (1738–1748)
making_significance: Royal excavations recovered Roman furniture, bronzes and wall paintings, whose publication fed Neoclassical design.
leaves_out: the diggers and the damage done
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; public-domain primary texts; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Nader Shah's sack of Delhi (1739)
making_significance: Nader Shah looted Delhi and took the Mughal treasury, including the Peacock Throne and major gems, to Iran.
leaves_out: the people killed in the massacre

name: Lisbon earthquake (1755)
making_significance: After the earthquake and fire, Lisbon was rebuilt with the Pombaline timber cage (gaiola) for quake resistance and standard building parts.
leaves_out: the poor displaced by the new plan

name: Battle of Plassey (1757)
other_names: East India Company rule in Bengal
making_significance: The Company's victory gave it control over Bengal's revenue and weaving districts, where it forced weavers into fixed contracts.
leaves_out: the weavers, spinners and dyers
free_sources: British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons); Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images)
notes: links: INS030; POL200. "Coerced weavers" follows Company records; degree debated.

name: Spinning jenny (c. 1764)
making_significance: James Hargreaves's multi-spindle wheel let one spinner work many threads, moving spinning from single wheels to machines.
leaves_out: women hand-spinners who lost work
free_sources: Science Museum Group Collection (link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Konbaung sack of Ayutthaya (1767)
making_significance: Burmese forces destroyed Ayutthaya and took artisans, dancers and scholars to Burma.
leaves_out: the deported artisans

name: Cook's voyages (1768–1779)
making_significance: Collections made on Cook's voyages sent Pacific barkcloth, featherwork and carvings to European museums, often without clear consent.
leaves_out: Pacific makers and exchange partners
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (per-item; taonga restricted); Wikimedia Commons; collection search link-out only

name: Water frame and Cromford Mill (1769–1771)
making_significance: Richard Arkwright's water-powered spinning frame and mill at Cromford set the model of the factory with shifts and child workers.
leaves_out: child workers and the inventors Arkwright borrowed from
free_sources: Science Museum Group Collection (link-out); Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images)

name: Siku quanshu and the literary inquisition (1772–1782)
other_names: Complete Library of the Four Treasuries
making_significance: The Qianlong emperor's great manuscript compilation also led to the banning and burning of thousands of titles judged hostile.
leaves_out: the many copyists
free_sources: Chinese Text Project (link-out); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data (CC BY 4.0)

name: Túpac Amaru II rebellion and ban on Inca dress (1780–1781)
making_significance: After the rebellion, Spanish officials banned Inca noble dress, portraits of Inca kings and other emblems of Inca descent.
leaves_out: Andean nobles who hid their textiles
notes: links: STY066; SCH004. Orders issued by Visitador Areche.

name: Calico Printers' Act (1787)
other_names: Designing and Printing of Linens Act
making_significance: British law gave textile print designers two months' copyright, an early design right for patterns.
leaves_out: designers in pattern shops
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Wedgwood anti-slavery medallion (1787)
other_names: "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?"
making_significance: Josiah Wedgwood's factory produced a jasperware medallion of a kneeling enslaved man for the abolition campaign, an early mass-made campaign object.
defined_by: abolitionists (Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade)
leaves_out: the self-image of enslaved people
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated); Wikimedia Commons
notes: links: NET035. Designer attributed to Henry Webber or William Hackwood.

name: Brookes slave ship diagram (1788)
making_significance: An abolitionist print showed enslaved Africans packed into the ship Brookes and was reproduced widely.
leaves_out: the voices of enslaved people
free_sources: Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain); British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons)

name: US Patent Act (1790)
making_significance: The first US federal patent law set up examined patents for useful inventions.
leaves_out: enslaved inventors, who could not hold patents
free_sources: US National Archives Catalog; Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated)

name: Abolition of guilds in France (1791)
other_names: Allarde decree; décret d'Allarde; Le Chapelier Law
making_significance: Revolutionary laws abolished the craft guilds and banned workers' combinations, opening trades to anyone with a licence.
leaves_out: journeymen's associations (compagnonnage)

name: Cotton gin (1793)
making_significance: The cotton gin made short-staple cotton profitable to clean, driving the expansion of slavery in the US South and raw cotton for mills.
leaves_out: the enslaved people who grew and picked cotton; earlier gins
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated); US National Archives Catalog

name: Opening of the Louvre (1793)
making_significance: The revolutionary state opened royal and church collections to the public, the model for national museums fed later by conquest.
leaves_out: the confiscated owners and later the looted

name: Napoleonic art seizures (1796–1815)
making_significance: French armies took paintings, sculpture and manuscripts from Italy, the Low Countries and elsewhere to Paris under treaty terms.
leaves_out: the places stripped of works
notes: Many works were returned in 1815, with Antonio Canova negotiating for the Papal States.

name: French campaign in Egypt (1798–1801)
making_significance: Napoleon's scholars surveyed Egypt and published the Description de l'Égypte, which fed the Egyptian Revival.
leaves_out: Egyptian scholars and workers

name: Siege of Seringapatam (1799)
making_significance: British forces killed Tipu Sultan and looted his palace, sending arms, textiles and Tipu's Tiger to Britain.
leaves_out: Mysore's makers and courts
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Yale Center for British Art (public-domain images)

name: Capitulation of Alexandria and the Rosetta Stone (1801)
making_significance: Under the French surrender in Egypt, antiquities including the Rosetta Stone passed to Britain.
leaves_out: Egyptian claims to the stone

name: Elgin's removal of the Parthenon sculptures (1801–1812)
making_significance: Lord Elgin's agents removed about half the surviving Parthenon sculptures to Britain, and Greece's return request (formal since 1983) is still unresolved.
leaves_out: the Ottoman-era Athenian view
notes: links: INS051; POL117. Legality of Elgin's firman disputed.

name: Luddite machine-breaking (1811–1816)
making_significance: Textile workers smashed stocking frames and shearing machines that cut wages or skill, and Parliament made frame-breaking a capital crime.
leaves_out: the workers' own aims beyond "anti-machine"
free_sources: British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons); public-domain primary texts

name: Iconoclasm in the Society and Austral Islands (1815–1820s)
making_significance: After conversions, islanders under missionary influence burned or gave up god images, some sent to London as trophies of conversion.
leaves_out: Islanders' own reasons for conversion
notes: links: POL087. Rurutu islanders gave up A'a and other figures to LMS missionaries on Ra'iatea in August 1821; A'a reached London in 1822.

name: French Artistic Mission to Brazil (1816)
making_significance: French artists invited to Rio de Janeiro founded academic art teaching in Brazil.
leaves_out: Afro-Brazilian craftsmen already working in Rio
free_sources: BNDigital (Biblioteca Nacional do Brasil); Wikimedia Commons

name: Abolition of the kapu system (1819)
making_significance: After Kamehameha I's death, rulers ended the kapu system and many heiau images were destroyed or hidden.
leaves_out: Hawaiians who kept images
free_sources: Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated); Wikimedia Commons

name: Clothing law of Mahmud II (1829)
making_significance: Ottoman law replaced turbans with the fez for officials, spreading fez-making and European tailoring.
leaves_out: women's dress, not covered

name: Cultivation System (1830–1870)
making_significance: The Dutch forced Javanese villages to grow indigo, sugar and coffee for export.
leaves_out: the Javanese villagers
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (CC0/PDM); Tropenmuseum images on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

name: Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears (1830–1839)
making_significance: US removal of Cherokee, Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole peoples tore makers from lands and materials.
leaves_out: those who resisted or hid
free_sources: US National Archives Catalog; Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain)

name: Slavery Abolition Act (1833)
making_significance: British law ended slavery in most colonies, paid compensation to enslavers and brought in indentured labour.
leaves_out: the formerly enslaved, who got nothing
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); SlaveVoyages (historical data public domain)

name: First Opium War and Treaty of Nanjing (1839–1842)
making_significance: The war opened five treaty ports and ceded Hong Kong, reorganising the old Canton trade in export painting, porcelain and silk.
leaves_out: Chinese opium users and traders

name: Treaty of Waitangi (1840)
making_significance: The treaty between the British Crown and Māori chiefs guaranteed Māori authority over their taonga, the basis for later claims over carvings, designs and knowledge.
defined_by: British Crown; Māori rangatira; Waitangi Tribunal (from 1975)
leaves_out: the differences between the English and Māori texts
free_sources: DigitalNZ; Te Papa Collections Online (per-item; taonga restricted)

name: Tenpō reforms (1841–1843)
making_significance: Shogunal reforms banned luxury and restricted prints of kabuki actors and courtesans, pushing ukiyo-e artists to new subjects.
leaves_out: censored publishers
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0); Art Institute of Chicago (CC0 public-domain works)

name: Irish Famine and crochet relief (1845–1852)
making_significance: During the famine, schemes taught women crochet and lace so they could earn, the start of "Irish crochet".
leaves_out: the women makers

name: Fortune's tea smuggling (1848–1851)
other_names: transfer of tea plants to India
making_significance: Robert Fortune took tea plants, seeds and workers from China to India for the East India Company.
leaves_out: the Chinese workers who went
free_sources: Wellcome Collection; British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons)

name: Treaty of Lahore and the Koh-i-Noor (1849)
making_significance: The Koh-i-Noor passed to Queen Victoria under the Treaty of Lahore and was recut in 1852.
leaves_out: India, Pakistan and Afghanistan's claims

name: Perry expeditions and the opening of Japan (1853–1858)
making_significance: US naval pressure forced Japan to open ports, and the export of lacquer, ceramics, fans and prints that followed fed Japonisme in Europe and America.
leaves_out: Japanese merchants and makers who shaped the export trade
free_sources: Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Bessemer process (1856)
making_significance: Henry Bessemer's converter blew air through molten pig iron to make cheap steel in bulk, used for rails, ships and later building frames.
leaves_out: William Kelly's parallel US work and older Asian crucible and co-fusion steels
free_sources: Science Museum Group Collection (link-out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Perkin's mauve (1856)
making_significance: William Perkin's aniline dye, found while trying to make quinine, began the coal-tar dye industry that displaced plant and insect dyes and the dyers who worked with them.
leaves_out: natural-dye growers and dyers worldwide
free_sources: Science Museum Group Collection (link-out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: Pair with alizarin (1868–69) and indigo (1897) rows.

name: Indian uprising and the looting of Delhi and Lucknow (1857–1858)
making_significance: After retaking Delhi and Lucknow, British troops looted palaces and houses, and Mughal manuscripts, jewels and arms entered British collections.
leaves_out: the many Indians killed in reprisals
free_sources: British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons); Wikimedia Commons

name: Indigo revolt (1859–1860)
making_significance: Bengal peasants refused to grow indigo under European planters' coercive contracts, and the protest weakened the Bengal indigo system before synthetic indigo ended it.
leaves_out: the peasants, especially women, in planters' records

name: Looting of the Summer Palace (1860)
making_significance: British and French troops looted and then burned the Yuanmingyuan in Beijing, and its enamels, jades, porcelain and bronze zodiac heads went to European collections and markets.
leaves_out: Chinese palace staff and craftsmen; China's continuing claims
notes: links: POL169. Context: Second Opium War (1856–1860).

name: Cotton famine (1861–1865)
making_significance: The US Civil War cut raw cotton to Lancashire mills, throwing mill workers out of work and pushing cotton growing in India and Egypt.
leaves_out: the enslaved growers whose labour supplied the pre-war mills
free_sources: British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons); Library of Congress (per-item rights; many public domain)

name: Blackbirding in the Pacific (1863–1904)
making_significance: Recruiters took Islanders, often by deception or force, to work on Queensland and Fijian plantations, taking makers out of their communities.
leaves_out: the Islanders' own accounts
notes: Deportations under the Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901 ended it.

name: Hwéeldi and the Long Walk (1863–1868)
other_names: Long Walk of the Navajo; Bosque Redondo
making_significance: US forced removal of the Diné to Bosque Redondo (Hwéeldi); after 1868 weavers gained access to brightly coloured manufactured yarns, and later reservation trading posts reshaped Diné weaving for the market.
leaves_out: those who died on the walk
free_sources: US National Archives Catalog; Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where designated)

name: Jiangnan Arsenal (1865)
making_significance: The Qing Self-Strengthening movement set up an arsenal in Shanghai to make guns and steamships, with a translation bureau for Western technical books.
leaves_out: the Chinese workers and foreign technicians

name: Return of the Oegyujanggak uigwe (2011)
making_significance: French troops took Joseon royal protocol books from Ganghwa Island in 1866, and France returned 297 volumes to Korea on renewable loan in 2011.
leaves_out: other Korean objects still abroad
notes: links: TXT106. Number of volumes to verify.

name: Exposition Universelle (Paris 1867)
making_significance: Japan took part officially for the first time, with Satsuma exhibiting separately, and the displays fed French Japonisme.
leaves_out: the Japanese makers named only by region

name: Removal of Te Hau ki Tūranga (1867)
making_significance: The Crown removed the carved meeting house Te Hau ki Tūranga, made under Raharuhi Rukupō in 1842, from Manutūke to Wellington, where it is now at Te Papa.
leaves_out: Rongowhakaata, the house's people
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (per-item; taonga restricted)
notes: Ownership recognised in the Rongowhakaata settlement; details to verify.

name: Alizarin synthesis (1868–1869)
making_significance: Graebe and Liebermann's synthesis of alizarin replaced madder root, and madder growing in France and the Netherlands collapsed within a few years.
leaves_out: madder growers and Turkey-red dyers

name: Maqdala (1868)
making_significance: After defeating Emperor Tewodros II, British troops looted Maqdala and took manuscripts, crosses, crowns and tabots to Britain.
leaves_out: the Ethiopian clergy and makers
free_sources: British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons); Wikimedia Commons

name: Removal of Hoa Hakananai'a (1868)
making_significance: Crew of HMS Topaze took the moai Hoa Hakananai'a from Rapa Nui; a Rapa Nui delegation asked for its return in 2018.
leaves_out: the Rapa Nui, who have asked for it back

name: Separation of Shinto and Buddhism (1868)
making_significance: Meiji orders to separate Shinto from Buddhism set off the destruction and sale of Buddhist images and temple treasures, many of which went abroad.
leaves_out: the temples and villages that lost their images
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Burning of the royal sampy (1869)
making_significance: After Queen Ranavalona II's conversion, the royal sampy (talismans of the Merina monarchy) were burned.
leaves_out: Malagasy people who kept ancestral practice

name: Ottoman antiquities regulations (1869–1884)
making_significance: Ottoman antiquities regulations, tightened in 1884 under Osman Hamdi Bey, made finds state property and banned export.
leaves_out: local finders; the empire's non-Turkish peoples

name: Suez Canal (1869)
making_significance: The canal cut the sea route between Europe and Asia, speeding trade in raw materials and manufactured goods.
leaves_out: the Egyptian corvée workers who dug it

name: Ban on Ainu tattooing and earrings (1871)
making_significance: Japan's Hokkaido Development Commission banned Ainu women's tattooing and men's earrings as part of assimilation.
leaves_out: Ainu, whose practices continued in secret

name: Meiji dress and hair reforms (1871–1872)
making_significance: Meiji edicts allowed men to cut the topknot and made Western-style dress official court and uniform wear, creating demand for tailoring and hats.
leaves_out: women, who kept kimono longer
free_sources: NDL Digital Collections (public-domain items); ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms)

name: Sagrenti War and the looting of Kumasi (1874)
making_significance: British troops looted Kumasi and took Asante gold regalia, some auctioned in London.
leaves_out: Asante goldsmiths and court

name: Haitōrei (1876)
making_significance: The ban on wearing swords in public ended demand for new swords, and sword-fitting makers turned to export metalwork.
leaves_out: the smiths who left the trade
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Wickham's rubber seeds (1876)
making_significance: Henry Wickham took about 70,000 Hevea seeds from Brazil to Kew, and seedlings started rubber plantations in Southeast Asia.
leaves_out: Indigenous knowledge of rubber

name: Ancient Monuments Protection Act (1882)
making_significance: Britain's first heritage law listed prehistoric monuments for state guardianship, with Augustus Pitt-Rivers as first inspector.
leaves_out: sites not on the schedule
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Code of Indian Offenses (1883)
making_significance: US rules banned Native American ceremonies, including dances and giveaways, pushing ritual making underground.
leaves_out: the communities who kept ceremonies

name: Krakatoa eruption (1883)
making_significance: News of the eruption spread worldwide by telegraph within days, and its ash coloured sunsets painted and reported far away.
leaves_out: the tens of thousands killed by tsunamis in Java and Sumatra
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; British Library public-domain images (Flickr Commons)
notes: Link to specific paintings (e.g. Munch) is speculative; keep it general.

name: Paris Convention (1883)
other_names: Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property
making_significance: The first international treaty on patents, trademarks and industrial designs let makers claim protection across member states.
leaves_out: colonised makers with no standing
free_sources: UNESCO/UN instrument texts (link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Berlin Conference (1884–1885)
making_significance: European powers set rules for claiming African territory, the framework for colonial extraction of rubber, ivory and craft.
leaves_out: all African states, which were absent

name: Potlatch ban (1884–1951)
making_significance: Canadian law banned the potlatch, criminalising ceremonies where masks, coppers and regalia were made and given.
leaves_out: Kwakwakaʼwakw and other nations who continued in secret

name: Third Anglo-Burmese War and the Mandalay regalia (1885)
making_significance: British forces deposed King Thibaw and took the Mandalay regalia, part of which the V&A returned to Burma in 1964.
leaves_out: Burmese court makers

name: Berne Convention (1886)
other_names: Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works
making_significance: The treaty extended copyright to authors and artists across member states without registration.
leaves_out: oral and collective traditions
free_sources: UNESCO/UN instrument texts (link-out); public-domain primary texts

name: Hall–Héroult process (1886)
making_significance: Independent discovery of electrolytic smelting made aluminium cheap enough for household goods and aircraft.
leaves_out: bauxite miners

name: Merchandise Marks Act (1887)
making_significance: British law required foreign goods to be marked with their origin, and "Made in Germany" became a mark of quality.
leaves_out: makers inside Britain who copied
free_sources: official text of the law (government legislation site; link-out)

name: Lei Áurea (1888)
making_significance: Brazil abolished slavery, the last country in the Americas to do so, ending the legal basis of enslaved labour in its plantations, mines and craft workshops.
leaves_out: those freed without land or pay

notes: links: POL015; CIV005. 2026 handover also returned ancestral human remains.

name: Imperial Household Artists (1890)
making_significance: The Meiji court appointed leading artists and craftsmen as Imperial Household Artists, backing metalwork, lacquer and ceramics.
leaves_out: workshop assistants
free_sources: ColBase (Japan Government Standard Terms); Met Open Access (CC0)

name: French conquest of Abomey (1892)
making_significance: French troops took the royal statues, thrones and doors of Abomey to Paris.
leaves_out: Fon court artists
free_sources: Paris Musées (Open Content); collection search link-out only

name: Lombok expedition (1894)
making_significance: Dutch forces looted the Cakranegara palace on Lombok, taking gold and jewellery.
leaves_out: Balinese and Sasak people
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (CC0/PDM); Tropenmuseum images on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

name: Danballyeong (1895)
making_significance: A Korean ordinance ordered men to cut the topknot, provoking protest and undermining the market for the horsehair hats (gat) and headbands worn with it.
leaves_out: women, who were not covered, and the protesters who resisted
free_sources: KOGL Type 1 images on Wikimedia Commons

name: Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law (1897)
making_significance: Japan's first national heritage law funded temple repairs and created "national treasures".
leaves_out: non-temple craft

name: British invasion and looting of Benin City (1897; the British "punitive expedition")
other_names: Sack of Benin City; Siege of Benin (Cleveland's records); Benin Massacre of 1897 (Nigeria's 2023 declaration)

name: Xinhai Revolution and the end of Qing dress (1911–1912)

name: Export of the Nefertiti bust (1913)

name: Werkbund debate (1914)

leaves_out: the workers who made the products

name: Armenian genocide (1915–1923)

name: Dazzle camouflage (1917)
making_significance: Artists led by Norman Wilkinson painted Allied ships in broken, high-contrast patterns meant to confuse enemy range-finding, turning painters and women's design teams to war work.
leaves_out: the women art students who drew most of the schemes

name: Hujum (1927)

name: Kazakh famine and forced sedentarisation (1930–1933)

name: Salt March (1930)
making_significance: Gandhi's march to Dandi to make salt from seawater broke the British salt monopoly in public and made a simple act of making into protest.

name: Mission Dakar–Djibouti (1931–1933)

leaves_out: Iraqi staff and residents who hid objects

name: Al Mahdi conviction at the ICC (2016)
other_names: Prosecutor v. Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi
making_significance: The International Criminal Court convicted a man for directing attacks on Timbuktu's mausoleums, its first case centred on cultural destruction.
leaves_out: other perpetrators

name: National Museum of Brazil fire (2018)
making_significance: Fire destroyed most of Brazil's National Museum in Rio, including Indigenous collections and recordings of languages.
leaves_out: the Indigenous communities whose objects were lost

name: Sarr–Savoy report (2018)
other_names: The Restitution of African Cultural Heritage: Toward a New Relational Ethics
making_significance: Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy recommended the return of African objects taken to France in the colonial period without proven consent.
leaves_out: museums outside France and objects acquired after independence
notes: Commissioned after Macron's Ouagadougou speech (28 November 2017).

name: Ainu Promotion Act (2019)
other_names: Act Promoting Measures to Realise a Society in Which the Pride of the Ainu People Is Respected
making_significance: Japanese law recognised the Ainu as an Indigenous people and funded culture programmes, including the Upopoy national museum.
leaves_out: Ainu calls for land and fishing rights

name: Notre-Dame fire (2019)
making_significance: Fire destroyed the cathedral's timber roof and spire, which were rebuilt with oak and hand-hewing methods like the medieval ones.
leaves_out: the workers exposed to lead

name: COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2023)
making_significance: The pandemic stopped factories and shipping, cancelled garment orders and saw home sewers and makerspaces produce masks and face shields.
leaves_out: garment workers left unpaid when orders were cancelled

name: French restitution law (2020)
making_significance: A French law allowed 26 objects from the royal treasures of Abomey to go to Benin and a sabre attributed to El Hadj Umar Tall to go to Senegal.
leaves_out: other objects that need a new law each time

name: Benin bronze returns by UK universities (2021)
making_significance: The University of Aberdeen returned a Benin head and Jesus College, Cambridge returned the cockerel Okukor, the first UK institutional returns.
leaves_out: objects in national museums bound by law

name: Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (2021)
making_significance: US law presumes goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang involve forced labour and bars their import unless proven otherwise, reaching cotton, garments and solar parts.
leaves_out: Uyghur workers themselves, who are rarely heard

name: German transfer of Benin bronzes (2022)
making_significance: Germany transferred ownership of Benin objects in its public museums to Nigeria and handed over the first 20 in Abuja.
leaves_out: the Benin court's own claims, raised later
notes: links: INS082; DYN038. Count of first handover to verify. A 2023 Nigerian presidential notice vested returned objects in the Oba of Benin.

name: Smithsonian and Horniman Benin returns (2022)
making_significance: The Smithsonian transferred 29 Benin objects to Nigeria and London's Horniman Museum 72, among the first transfers of ownership by national museums outside Germany.
defined_by: museum trustees; Nigerian National Commission for Museums and Monuments
leaves_out: objects in museums barred by law from returning

name: Dutch returns to Indonesia and Sri Lanka (2023)
making_significance: The Netherlands returned 478 objects, including part of the Lombok treasure and Singhasari statues to Indonesia and a jewelled cannon to Sri Lanka.
leaves_out: claims from other former colonies

name: Asante gold loans to Kumasi (2024)
date_note: loans announced January 2024; display opened 1 May 2024
making_significance: The V&A (17 objects) and British Museum (15) lent 32 Asante gold and regalia objects, many taken in the wars of 1874 and 1895-96, to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi for three years, extendable by three.
leaves_out: the question of ownership, left open by a loan

name: EU Right to Repair Directive (2024)
other_names: Directive on common rules promoting the repair of goods
making_significance: The EU obliged manufacturers of some appliances to offer repair at reasonable prices and to supply parts.
leaves_out: repairers outside the EU

name: Revised NAGPRA regulations (2024)
making_significance: New US rules required museums to get consent from tribes before displaying or researching covered items, and many closed displays.
leaves_out: tribes without federal recognition
